name: Genetic Algorithm (GA)
analogy: Think of it as breeding racehorses. You let the fastest animals mate, mix their traits, occasionally allow a random mutation, and keep the champion of each generation. After many generations the stable is full of fast horses that no one designed by hand.

steps.title: Write each candidate as a string of genes
steps.description: Every candidate solution is encoded as a fixed row of values, like a chromosome. For a yes-or-no choice each position is a 1 or a 0, so one row describes a whole combination.
steps.inExample: There are 12 candidate indicators. A candidate is a row of 12 ones and zeros, where a 1 means that indicator is used.

steps.title: Score every candidate
steps.description: Each candidate gets a fitness number from a test, for example a validation score with a small penalty for using many items. Fitter candidates will be more likely to become parents.
steps.inExample: Each row trains a quick classifier on its chosen indicators and gets a validation score, minus a small penalty per indicator used.

steps.title: Pick parents by small tournaments
steps.description: To choose a parent, draw a few candidates at random and take the fittest of them. This favours good candidates without letting one dominate completely.
steps.inExample: Three random rows are drawn and the one with the best score becomes parent A; the same is repeated for parent B.

steps.title: Cross the parents over
steps.description: Cut both parents at a point and join the first part of one to the second part of the other. Pieces that worked well in each parent can end up together in the child.
steps.inExample: Parent A uses indicators 1, 3, 6, 10 and 11; parent B uses 2, 3, 7, 10 and 12. Cutting after position 6 gives a child using 1, 3, 6, 7, 10 and 12.

steps.title: Mutate a little
steps.description: Each gene has a small chance of flipping. Mutation brings in choices that no parent had and keeps the group from becoming identical too early.
steps.inExample: With a 2 percent flip chance per position, roughly one child in five, with 12 positions each, has at least one indicator switched on or off.

steps.title: Keep the champion and repeat
steps.description: The best candidate or two is copied unchanged into the next generation so progress is never lost. The cycle repeats until the best score stops improving.
steps.inExample: After about 40 generations the best row has settled on a set of 5 indicators and stopped changing.

useFor.example: Selecting which of 12 candidate indicators to feed an MNQ direction model, rewarding validation score and penalising redundant ones.
Trying combinations of entry filter, exit rule and time-of-day window, each with integer settings, against a backtest.
Letting tree-shaped formulas built from open, high, low, close and volume compete, in the style of genetic programming.

useFor.task: Trading off several goals at once
useFor.example: Keeping a family of strategy variants that balance return, maximum drawdown and turnover instead of one winner.

avoidWhen: All the settings are smooth numbers and a slope is available; gradient descent is faster and more exact.
The fitness test is noisy and cheap to overfit; the search will find combinations that merely fit the noise, so a held-out test is essential or a simpler method is safer.

example.scenario: A researcher wants a small, non-redundant set of indicators for an MNQ 5-minute direction model, chosen from 12 candidates, and lets a genetic search do the choosing.

input.summary: The pool of candidates, the size of the population and the search settings.

fields.name: candidate indicators
fields.meaning: Including relative strength index, average true range, volume ratio and distance from the 50-bar average.

fields.name: population size
fields.meaning: How many indicator combinations are alive in each generation.

fields.name: tournament size
fields.meaning: How many random candidates compete to become a parent.

fields.name: mutation chance per position
fields.meaning: Chance that an indicator is switched on or off in a child.

fields.name: penalty per indicator used
fields.value: two tenths of a percentage point
fields.meaning: Subtracted from the validation score so that smaller sets are favoured.

fields.name: generations
fields.meaning: How many rounds of selection, crossover and mutation are run.

output.summary: The best indicator set found and its fitness.

fields.name: chosen indicators
fields.value: relative strength index, average true range, volume ratio, 50-bar distance, 6-bar return
fields.meaning: The indicators switched on in the best row.

fields.name: validation score
fields.meaning: Area under the receiver operating characteristic curve on validation folds, where 50 percent is no ranking skill.

fields.name: fitness after penalty
fields.meaning: Validation score minus 5 indicators times two tenths of a point, which is one point.

example.reading: A validation score of 54 percent is a slight lean, not a strong signal. The set was chosen because it scored well on those folds, so measure it again on later data. If a rerun with a different random seed picks a very different set, the score surface is flat and the choice is mostly noise.
